citation: libghostty-vt is the encoder; ghostty src/input/function_keys.zig:199 for the shift+enter entry. Cross-checkable against herdr tests/fixtures/keyboard_protocol_corpus.tsv, which encodes the same protocol from Rust.
why:
The encoder is libghostty-vt's, so these do not test escape-sequence generation - upstream does that, and a second implementation written to agree with it would be the bug. What they pin is everything around it that is ours: that the modifier bits still line up with the ABI they are cast to, that a mode profile actually reaches the encoder, that a composing keystroke stays out of the pane, and what the conservative default costs in bytes.

The broad survey of common keys lives as a rendered snapshot (Tests/MusterVTTests/snapshots/keys-*.txt) rather than as cases here, because it is one matrix with one reason rather than nineteen behaviors, and its oracle is upstream. A port reproduces the same rendering. Kan a_27Haa38Gp carries moving its keystroke list into data.

cases.name: enter is a carriage return under the conservative default
cases.why: The baseline for the case below. Enter is submit in every agent harness, so if these bytes are wrong the pane is unusable rather than degraded.

cases.name: shift+enter survives the conservative default
cases.why: The distinction an agent needs most - newline versus submit - and the one the plan assumed would be the first casualty of guessing low. It is not: ghostty encodes shift+enter as a fixterms sequence in every mode, not only under kitty (function_keys.zig:199, an entry with no mode qualifier). So an agent can still tell them apart through a pane Muster knows nothing about, which is why the mode guess was acceptable to ship.

cases.name: an arrow without application cursor mode is a CSI sequence
cases.why: Half of the one guess that breaks a program rather than degrading it. This is what a power-on terminal expects.

cases.name: application cursor mode changes what an arrow sends
cases.why: The other half, and the reason bare arrows are routed to the daemon instead of encoded here. vim and less put the cursor keys in application mode - less calls smkx on startup - and a client that guesses wrong sends a sequence the program does not recognize. That the profile changes the output at all is what this pins: a profile that never reached the encoder would produce CSI here and look fine in every other case.

cases.name: a composing keystroke never reaches the pane
cases.why: Mid-composition the keystroke belongs to the input method. Sending it too would deliver the romaji alongside whatever it composes into - the same doubling shape as the bug that made typing `hello` produce `hheelllloo`.

cases.name: ctrl+c is the interrupt byte
cases.why: Modifiers is declared to match the encoder's ABI so the seam is a cast rather than a translation. If a dependency bump renumbers those bits, every chord silently encodes as a different one - and ctrl+c becoming something else is the failure a user hits within a minute.

cases.name: ctrl+a is its own control byte
cases.why: The pair of ctrl+c. One chord could match by luck after a bit renumbering; two adjacent ones passing means the bits line up rather than collide.

cases.name: option composes text rather than sending alt, by default
cases.why: The macOS default, and the reason this is not simply `alt sends escape`. Option is a composing key on this platform, so a Mac user pressing option+e expects an accent rather than a meta chord. With the setting off, the alt bit is dropped and the text the layout produced stands alone.

cases.name: option configured as alt sends the escape prefix instead
cases.why: What a user who lives in readline turns on. The same keystroke has to produce a different answer under a different profile, which is the second proof that profile settings reach the encoder rather than being stored and ignored.

cases.name: the real keystroke: opt+t composes a dagger by default
cases.why: The concrete cost of the macOS default, in the keystroke somebody actually pressed. A US layout turns option+t into U+2020, so with the setting off the pane receives that character and an agent bound to alt+t never hears about it. Recorded as a case because the two abstract cases above use a key whose composed form is itself, which hides exactly this.

cases.name: opt+t under left-option-as-alt is a meta chord
cases.why: The same keystroke, the setting a person turns on, and the answer their agent is waiting for. This pair is the whole justification for the config key: nothing about the keystroke changes, only what Muster was told option means.

cases.name: the other option key still composes under leftOnly
cases.why: Why the setting is four-valued rather than a flag. Somebody who picks a side wants meta chords on one hand and accented characters on the other, so a per-side setting that ignored the side would be indistinguishable from `always` and would quietly cost them their accents.

cases.name: rightOnly is the mirror of leftOnly, on the same keystroke
cases.why: The two per-side values have to be told apart by which side is held rather than by which is named, and a case for only one of them would pass on an encoder that treated both as `always`.

cases.name: a shifted option chord keeps its shift
cases.why: Why the shell reports what the layout would have produced without option, rather than the core reusing `unshiftedCodepoint`. That field is unshifted by definition, so falling back to it turns opt+shift+t into a lowercase meta chord - readline's alt+F and alt+f are different commands, so the difference is not cosmetic. Only the layout can answer what the other reading was, which is why it is reported rather than derived.
